At 57A, growing up in all sorts of church sermons, bible camp, Sunday school, etc, I always heard that repentance is not *feeling* bad about something. It's the act of turning away from the thing you feel bad about and choosing a new way. Turning a new leaf. Conviction, confession, and repentance.

That said, I see that the dictionary attributes it to the feeling, not necessarily the action. It also told me that the root words in Greek and Hebrew, do seem to agree with what I learned about turning away from the error of your ways. It's funny how deeply that teaching stuck with me... To the degree that I was kind of flummoxed by the clue. 

My apologies for looking up the word in the dictionary first and not ending with: do better NYT!  😏  Maybe next nitweek... Har!!

Found online:

"Check (also checker, Brit: chequer, dicing, or checkerboard and checkerboard pattern) is a pattern of modified stripes consisting of crossed horizontal and vertical lines which form squares. The pattern typically contains two colours where a single checker (that is a single square within the check pattern) is surrounded on all four sides by a checker of a different colour."

and

"A plaid is a printed or woven fabric composed of an array of intersecting vertical and horizontal stripes in varying widths and colours. In contrast to checks, plaid fabrics are more intricate, featuring asymmetrical or irregular patterns."

One distinguishing factor: if checks are black and white, plaids would be black, white, and grey where the intersecting black and white woven threads form the in-between grey color.

I always start with Across, and after awhile a couple of things emerged in my mind: one, something felt similarly odd about every clue, and two, not one of them immediately tipped me to an answer, which by the bottom third of the puzzle on a Thursday is quite unusual for me. It was a very weird feeling to know that I could of course read the words and understand their individual meanings but could not parse the clues in the way I can normally. If nothing else, it was an *outstanding* reminder that an enormous portion of crossword solving is down to practice, and that when you get in their rhythms and customs they shake open much more easily. (A milder version of this for those of us who habitually solve only the NYT puzzle is to try some other publication's crossword - different editing styles do change the experience!)

Anyway, I eventually caught on to the idea that all the clues seemed odd in the same approximate way, went on to try the "normal" Downs, and got help pretty quickly! What a good puzzle, and a fun, "bendy" start to the morning!
